```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, dpi = 80)
```

Every dataset in WeGrowHealthR comes from one generator, `wgh_simulate()`.
Real growth records of children cannot be shared, so the package ships
simulated cohorts instead. The `wgh_like` preset is set so that a cohort
**resembles** the published results of the school health cohort studied in
the research program (see `wgh_references()`): the same patterns, the same
directions of effect and numbers of a similar size. It does not reproduce
published values, and nothing computed from it is a finding.

This vignette explains how the generator works, how to check the
resemblance, how to change the simulated world, and how to use the truth
file to test methods.

## Simulating a cohort

```{r}
library(WeGrowHealthR)
sim <- wgh_simulate(20000, seed = 2026)
sim
```

The main arguments are:

* `n_children`, the number of children generated before enrolment rules
  (fewer appear in the visit data, because not every child attends),
* `preset`, `"wgh_like"` (default) or `"reference"` (a cohort with simple,
  textbook settings), or a settings list from `wgh_preset()`,
* `seed`, so the same call always gives the same cohort,
* `informative_visits`, whether attendance depends on the child's BMI as in
  real school data (`FALSE` makes visits missing at random),
* `style`, the column names: `"book1"` (`pid`, `yearvisit`, `baz`) or
  `"book2"` (`pid`, `schoolyear`, `bmiz`),
* `...`, single settings that override the preset, for example
  `years = 2012:2025`.

The result is a list:

```{r}
names(sim)
head(sim$visits)
```

* `visits` holds the measurements, one row per visit, with WHO z-scores,
* `roster` lists every child and school year, attended or not,
* `truth_child` and `truth_visit` hold the true values behind the
  measurements (next sections),
* `pop_peaks` the population APHV and PHV implied by the settings,
* `settings` the full settings used.

### How the children grow

Each child's height follows a Preece-Baines mean curve for the child's sex,
joined below 6 years to a WHO-shaped early childhood curve. The child's own
curve is the mean curve shifted in size, timing and intensity, as in a SITAR
model. Children belong to growth phenotypes (for example early and intense,
or late and gentle) that shift these parameters. Adiposity is a stable
child trait with a slow drift. It raises BMI, makes puberty slightly earlier
and is linked with height. BMI is converted to weight through the WHO
reference. Measurement error is added to height and weight. Attendance
depends on age, calendar year (with a year of school closures) and, when
`informative_visits = TRUE`, on BMI.

## How close is the resemblance?

`wgh_targets` lists published patterns with acceptable bands, for example
the prevalence of overweight and obesity by sex, the APHV of boys and girls
and the spread of individual timing. `wgh_resemblance_report()` computes
each pattern in a simulated cohort and checks it against its band.

```{r}
head(wgh_targets)
rr <- wgh_resemblance_report(sim)
rr
```

```{r, fig.alt = "Position of each simulated statistic within its acceptable band", fig.height = 6}
plot(rr, base_size = 9)
```

Each row of the plot is one pattern. The green area is the acceptable band,
the cross the published value and the dot the simulated value (blue inside
the band, orange outside). `plot(rr, only_failed = TRUE)` shows only the
patterns outside their band.

Some patterns were used to set the preset (`tuned = TRUE`). Others were kept
out as independent checks, for example the association between BMI and
height in childhood and in late adolescence. Passing those checks shows the
generator has the right structure, not only the right averages.

## Building another world

Because the true structure is known, you can change one setting and see how
an analysis responds. `wgh_preset()` returns all settings, with units
documented in the package source.

```{r}
s <- wgh_preset("wgh_like")
s$beta_tempo_adiposity
s$beta_tempo_adiposity <- c(Male = 0, Female = 0)     # adiposity no longer changes timing
alt <- wgh_simulate(5000, preset = s, seed = 1)
cor(alt$truth_child$u_adip, alt$truth_child$b_tempo)
cor(sim$truth_child$u_adip, sim$truth_child$b_tempo)
```

In the altered world, adiposity and timing are unrelated, while in the
default world children with more adiposity have earlier timing (negative
`b`). Running the pubertal spurt analysis on both worlds shows whether a
method can tell them apart.

`wgh_tune_preset()` adjusts a few settings automatically so that a preset
meets the prevalence and age-distribution targets, which is how the
`wgh_like` preset was set.

## The truth file: testing methods

`truth_child` holds each child's true SITAR parameters, phenotype and
adiposity, and `truth_visit` the true height and velocity at each visit.

```{r}
head(sim$truth_child)
```

`wgh_truth_check()` compares estimates with the truth, for example the
individual APHV from a SITAR model with `aphv_true`:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
boys <- sim$visits[sim$visits$sex == "Male", ]
fit <- wgh_fit_sitar(boys, df = 5, age_range = c(6, 18))
eff <- wgh_sitar_effects(fit)
eff$pid <- eff$id
wgh_truth_check(eff, sim$truth_child, est_col = "aphv", truth_col = "aphv_true")
```

This is the safest way to learn what a method can and cannot recover.

## Bundled datasets

| Dataset | What it is |
|---|---|
| `growdat` | A cohort of about 3,300 children from 18 months to 18 years, book 1 column names |
| `growdat_raw` | `growdat` as a messy export, for practising cleaning |
| `growdat2_mini` | A smaller cohort with book 2 column names, with its truth file `growdat2_mini_truth` |
| `clinical_cases` | A few dozen children with clinical patterns (`wgh_simulate_clinical_cases()`) |
| `wgh_targets` | The published patterns used to check resemblance |
| `who_lms`, `cdc_lms` | WHO and CDC 2000 LMS reference tables |

The full-size cohort used in book 2 can be obtained with `wgh_download()`.
It downloads a frozen copy when a URL is configured, verifying its checksum,
and otherwise regenerates the same cohort locally. The result records where
it came from in its `"provenance"` attribute.

```{r}
small <- wgh_download(url = NULL, n_children = 500)
attr(small, "provenance")[c("source", "n_children", "seed", "preset", "package_version")]
```
